name: Licensing Synthetic Media
title: Licensing Synthetic Media
answer: Licensing synthetic media covers the rights to use, modify, distribute, and monetize outputs made by generative systems, plus the inputs and model weights that produce them. It spans images, video, audio, voice, text, and 3D assets, and it touches training data, prompts, adaptations, and the final file. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models and 1000 video models, which shows how many separate output pipelines can carry different license terms. The field sits inside rights and provenance in AI art, so it connects copyright, contract, publicity rights, and attribution.

crumbs.name: Rights and Provenance in AI Art

sections.body: Licensing synthetic media covers the rights to use, modify, distribute, and monetize outputs made by generative systems, plus the inputs and model weights that produce them. It spans images, video, audio, voice, text, and 3D assets, and it touches training data, prompts, adaptations, and the final file. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models and 1000 video models, which shows how many separate output pipelines can carry different license terms. The field sits inside rights and provenance in AI art, so it connects copyright, contract, publicity rights, and attribution.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What it runs on: model provider terms of service, open source and commercial model licenses, data set licenses, and rights clearance systems. Provenance infrastructure includes metadata standards, watermarking, asset registries, and audit logs that record model, version, prompt, and edits. Licensing synthetic media also depends on identity and likeness databases, voice consent records, and collective management organizations for music and text. In practice, these systems sit alongside digital asset management, contract lifecycle tools, and takedown or dispute workflows.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done: rights teams map each asset to its model, training data sources, and any third party inputs, then negotiate or apply license terms. They use opt out lists, data licensing deals, model cards, and output filters to reduce risk before release. For music and voice, consent and compensation terms are often handled through labels, publishers, unions, or voice actors. Provenance is captured at generation time and checked again at publication, with human review for high risk uses. The site tracks 2000 audio models, which shows why music and voice licensing is a major part of the work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance: the main questions are whether an output is copyrightable, whether it infringes training data or existing works, and whether it violates publicity, trademark, or moral rights. Contracts can shift risk through warranties, indemnities, and limitations of liability, but they do not settle ownership by themselves. Provenance records help show where an asset came from, what model made it, and what edits occurred, which matters in disputes and audits. Disclosure rules and platform policies may require labeling synthetic media, and some licenses restrict commercial use, political use, or impersonation. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services, as a live signal of unresolved questions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going: more standardized provenance, clearer model licenses, and broader collective licensing for training data and outputs. Regulators are moving toward transparency and labeling duties, while courts continue to shape what can be owned and what must be licensed. Growth is likely in consent based voice and likeness markets, output royalties, and automated rights clearance. The number of tracked models, 1000 image and 1000 video, suggests licensing will become more granular and more automated. The field will likely settle on a mix of contract, metadata, and collective rights rather than one global rule.
